newsitem.title: UK: Supply pressures Urals crude, Nigerian grades steady.
newsitem.headline: Supply pressures Urals crude, Nigerian grades steady.

text.p: Russian Urals crude was under pressure on Wednesday from ample supply with buyers kept at bay by negative refining margins, traders said.
They said a May 22-23 Urals was sold on Tuesday night by a trader to a Spanish refiner at a distressed Dated Brent -$1.38.
The deal was preceeded by a small May 27-29 loader (65,000-70,000 tonnes) of the sour crude reported sold at eight cents higher, or Dated Brent -$1.30.
Urals was assessed in the Dated Brent -$1.40/-$1.30 region with later barrels possibly worth more, compared with Tuesday's early buy/sell levels of Dated Brent -$1.25/-$1.15.
But one trader said the Dated Brent -$1.40 mark was the real market level, adding that earlier Urals deals this month at Dated Brent -$1.18 and -$1.15 proved this point.
"The market was artificially kept at higher levels," the trader added.
Traders said worsening refining margins from the sudden rise in North Sea Brent, which has gained some $2.50 since the start of May, kept buyers at bay.
Some eight Urals cargoes, mostly third decade May, were on offer on Tuesday and one seller was heard offering as far afield as the United States.

A lot of poeple would agree it (Urals) is going lower...I don't think they (differentials) have improved with the way Brent rushed up, Mediterranean refiners are seeing poor margins on the sour crudes," one trader said.
The seller of the first cargo said the market was depressed as there were many prompt barrels unsold, adding: "There are no firm buyers out there, there's only some potential buying interest."

Talks between Syria's state oil agency Sytrol and term lifters over the June prices continued. Traders said they doubted the Syrians would get the high Dated Brent -60 cents they are asking for Syrian Light.

"Buyers want a rollover from May (Dated Brent)-82 cents)...(Dated Brent) -60 cents sounds a bit ambitious but it sounds the Syrians know more about the Iraqi situation than perhaps a few others and that's why they're digging their heels in," one trader said.

On Tuesday, diplomats on the U.N. sanctions committee on Iraq said everything appeared to be on track for an extension of the "oil-for-food" deal when the current period ends June 7. But they said the U.S.remained cagey about its position.

The deal allows Iraq to export up to $2 billion dollars worth of oil every six months to buy food and medicine for Iraqis reeling under U.N. sanctions imposed on Iraq after its 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
One trader said the Urals market was confused, skittish and unable to find direction, adding there's a lot of concern about a rollover of Iraqi barrels.
"We are waiting for the United Nations to come out and say there is an automatic rollover," he added.

West African crude markets were quiet early on Wednesday with traders saying that deals have dried up with parties reluctant to report any prices ahead of the release of Nigeria's Official Selling Price for June.

But most traders said the grades seemed to be stable, with Bonny Light assessed around Dated Brent +48 cents and Forcados at about a 20 cents premium to Dated Brent. Traders have said Nigerian and Angolan barrels remained popular with Asian buyers who will be eyeing the market soon, but some said that the grades may suffer in the short term due to worsening refining margins.
